title: Hand a drink out a self-closing drive-thru window: hold the slider, set the cup on the outside shelf, let it shut clear
instruction: Serve the drink through the drive-thru window. With your left hand, slide the window open by its pull bar and hold it. With your right hand, carry the cup out through the opening and set it down upright on the shelf outside, then let go. Bring your right arm back inside, then let go of the window so it closes by itself without its edge touching either arm or the cup, and draw your left hand back.
context: Fast food and counter workers (O*NET 35-3023.00) have the Core task "Serve customers in eating places that specialize in fast service and inexpensive carry-out food." At the drive-thru the window shuts itself: Quikserv's SC-4030 is a self-closing slider, and "By simply releasing the window after serving the customer, the door panel closes automatically." So one hand holds the panel open against its pull while the other passes a full, lidded drink out and sets it on the hand-off shelf outside the window for the driver; in the task the shelf stands in for the driver's hand, so no person is within the robot's reach in a trial. Unlike a lid or a pusher held back, the panel's own closing path runs through the serving arm: the holding hand lets go only after the serving arm is back inside, or the panel strikes the arm or knocks the cup.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left); heights above the counter top, which is the station table. Wall: painted plywood on studs, 10 cm thick, inner face at x 36 and outer face at x 46, spanning y -60 to y 120 and 130 cm high. Set in it is a Quikserv SC-4030 self-closing slider: an aluminium frame 48 x 36 in (121.9 x 91.4 cm) in a rough opening of 48-3/8 x 36-3/8 in, its bottom rail 4 cm above the counter, spanning y -17.5 to y 104.4. Its service opening is 20-1/4 in wide by 29 in high (51.4 x 73.7 cm), spanning y -15 to y 36.4, its sill 12.9 cm up; to its left is a fixed pane of 1/4 in clear tempered glass. The sliding panel (1/4 in clear tempered glass in an anodized aluminium frame, about 55 x 77 cm and about 8 kg: 6.7 kg of glass from its size and thickness, plus the frame) hangs from a top track in the plane x 39, inside the fixed pane. Closed, its leading stile meets the right jamb at y -15. It slides toward +y behind the fixed pane, with up to 48 cm of travel. Its vertical pull bar (25 mm round aluminium, 30 cm long, from 20 to 50 cm above the counter, standing 3 cm off the glass) is on its inside face 3 cm from the stile. It closes by itself: in the simulation the pull is 10 N, with a damper (22 N s/m) so that it shuts from 30 cm open in about 1 s; both are settings, and a real trial reads the real panel's pull with a spring scale on the bar. The lock is not modelled; the window starts shut and unlocked. Outside, under the window on the outer wall: a stainless hand-off shelf (Ready Access 65198701, 13-gauge stainless, 53-1/2 x 10 in, listed for interior or exterior mounting), its top 12.5 cm up, reaching from x 46 to x 71.4 and spanning y -20 to y 116. Inside, on the counter at x 28, y -15: a 16 oz paper cold cup with a polystyrene flat lid, about 9 cm across the rim, 6 cm across the base and 14 cm tall, about 20 g empty and holding 0.47 kg of water. Both arms start at their home poses, grippers open. For the real trial, a side camera outside at x 52, y -45, 40 cm up looks along +y across the opening and the shelf (a prop in the simulation), and a second camera inside, above the right jamb, looks down onto the stile's face. Simplified: the cup and its water move as one rigid body; the panel's pull and damper are settings. Low-cost real-trial stand-in for the commercial window (about US$300 to 400 in total, an estimate and not a quote; the Quikserv SC-4030 is a sim-only reference), full steps in the README. It keeps every value the simulation uses: a 55 x 77 cm sash of about 8 kg (6 mm polycarbonate in aluminium angle plus 4.4 kg of steel flat bar, weighed and trimmed to 8.0 +/- 0.5 kg), 48 cm of travel set by track stops, a constant closing pull of 10 N (a 1.02 kg weight on a cord over a pulley, or a 10 N constant-force spring; never a gas spring), a damper of about 22 N s/m (an adjustable oil damper), and the 25 mm x 30 cm pull bar 3 cm off the glass. The wall is a timber frame with 18 mm plywood on both faces (10 cm thick) and the same opening; the sash hangs from a Hawa Junior 80/B top-hung track. Check before the trial: a spring scale on the bar reads 10 +/- 1 N at 0, 15, 30 and 45 cm of opening, and the time from 30 cm to shut is 1.0 +/- 0.3 s. The shelf can be any 53 x 10 in stainless or plywood shelf at the same height. Protect the grippers and the rig from water: the real cup holds 0.47 kg of water, so work over a rimmed tray (25 mm lip, 60 x 40 cm) on the counter and a second under the shelf, with a towel or absorbent mat in each; keep the wrist cable exits and the controller under plastic sleeving or a drip cover; keep the power strip and controller off the floor and out from under the shelf; use a lid with a snap-fit rim; and for the first trials fill the cup with 0.2 kg of water, then the full 0.47 kg once the carry is clean.
scoring: 0, latched, if the face of the panel's leading stile (the face that meets the jamb) ever touches the cup or any part of either arm, or the closing panel stops short of shut with no gripper's fingers on it (it rests on an arm or the cup), or the cup tips more than 30 degrees or falls (drops at 1 m/s or more, or ends off the shelf more than 3 cm below its top), or it is crushed (judged on the video: a dent in the cup wall deeper than 5 mm, read with a ruler laid across it, or water past the lid; in the simulation the cup is rigid, and a squeeze above 20 N, a setting, counts as crushing). A gripper holding the pull bar 3 cm from the stile is not a touch. Otherwise, judged at the end of the trial: 0.25, the panel was opened at least 15 cm at any time and the cup was lifted at least 2 cm off the counter at any time; 0.5, that, and the cup's centre is past the wall's outer face (x 46), upright within 15 degrees; 0.75, that, and the cup stands on the outside shelf (its base within 1 cm of the shelf top and wholly over it, upright within 15 degrees) and both grippers are at least 8 mm off it; 1.0, that, with both arms back inside the wall's inner face (x 36), the panel shut (gap under 5 mm) with neither hand on it, and the panel and cup still (no visible movement over 1 s on the video). Any other end state scores 0. Real trial: the two cameras' video for any touch by the stile's face, the cup's tilt and anything caught in the closing window; a tape on the sill for the 15 cm opening and the video for the 2 cm lift and the grippers' clearance; a photo of the cup on the shelf; a tape at the closed panel's edge. Check runs: one hand only, so the panel shuts as soon as it is let go: 0.25 at most; the panel let go while the right arm is still in the opening: 0; the panel held open at the end: 0.75.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at 240 Hz on GPU. The cup and its water are one rigid body: a spill is a tip past 30 degrees, crushing a squeeze over 20 N (settings; a real trial reads the dent and the video). The panel's 10 N closing pull and 22 N s/m damper are settings standing in for the closer; the lock is not modelled. The stile's touch is checked against capsules round the arms and fingertips. The low-cost real-trial window (README) has the same 8 kg, 48 cm travel, 10 N pull and damping.
